title: High-Protein Spinach Paneer Wrap Packs 26g Protein in 460 Calories
excerpt: Instagram food creator Shagun Malhotra shared her paneer wrap recipe on September 17 — spiced paneer slabs and crunchy vegetables inside a spinach-based wrap, aimed at vegetarians trying to stay fitter in their 30s and beyond.
body:
• Instagram food creator Shagun Malhotra, who runs the page My Food Project, shared her healthy paneer wrap recipe on September 17.
  • The wrap delivers 26 g of protein for 460 kcal, per the creator's own calculation — a strong number for a vegetarian meal built mostly around paneer.
  • The wrap itself is made by blending boiled spinach leaves with wheat flour, milk and one egg, then cooking the batter in a non-stick pan with a little butter or ghee.
  • Crisp-coated paneer slabs, sautéed onions and bell peppers, lettuce, tomato and cream cheese go inside; it works for breakfast, lunch, dinner or an evening snack.

A creator's recipe for eating fitter in her 30s

On September 17, Shagun Malhotra, the Instagram food creator behind the page My Food Project, posted a recipe she says she started eating herself to stay fitter in her 30s: a paneer wrap built on a green spinach wrap, masala-coated paneer and crunchy vegetables. "A colourful, crunchy, and wholesome wrap to help you be fitter in a yummy and happy way," she wrote. Hindustan Times, which reported the recipe, notes that its story is based on user-generated content and has not been independently verified — so the nutrition figures here are the creator's own claims, not lab-tested values.

Why the protein math matters for vegetarians

Protein is the hardest macro for many Indian vegetarians to hit, and most home-cooked meals land well short. A wrap claiming 26 g of protein in 460 kcal is genuinely competitive with a chicken-based equivalent, and it gets there honestly: 200 g of paneer alone carries roughly 36 g of protein in the raw ingredient, so 26 g in the finished, vegetable-bulked wrap is a plausible claim. The spinach wrap is the clever part — it replaces a refined-flour tortilla with a base that adds fiber, iron and folate for almost no extra calories, while the egg in the batter helps the wrap hold together and adds a few more grams of protein. At 460 kcal it sits comfortably in full-meal territory rather than snack territory, which matters for readers trying to eat one satisfying meal instead of grazing through the afternoon.

Ingredients

For the spiced paneer:

  • 200 g paneer, in one slab
  • ½ tsp haldi (turmeric) powder
  • 1 tsp red chilli powder
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp chaat masala

For the spinach wrap:

  • 30 spinach leaves, boiled
  • 1.5 tbsp wheat flour
  • ⅓ cup milk
  • 1 egg
  • 1 tsp black pepper powder
  • Salt to taste
  • A little butter or ghee, for cooking

For assembly:

  • Cream cheese
  • Lettuce leaves
  • Sliced onions
  • Sliced red and yellow bell peppers
  • Sliced tomato
  • A favourite dip, for serving

Method

  1. Spray oil in a hot pan, lay the 200 g paneer slab down and sprinkle the haldi, red chilli powder, salt and chaat masala over it. Coat the paneer evenly and cook until the outer coating turns crisp, then remove and cut into large rectangular slabs.
  2. Blend the boiled spinach leaves, wheat flour, milk, egg, black pepper powder and salt into a smooth paste.
  3. Cook this mixture in a non-stick pan with a little butter or ghee — it sets into a thin green wrap.
  4. Sauté the sliced onions, red and yellow bell peppers and capsicum in a spice mix of your choice until just tender.
  5. Assemble: spread cream cheese over the wrap, layer lettuce, the sautéed vegetables, the crisp paneer slabs and sliced tomatoes.
  6. Fold and serve with a favourite dip. It works as breakfast, lunch, dinner or an evening snack.

"A colourful, crunchy, and wholesome wrap to help you be fitter in a yummy and happy way."

— Shagun Malhotra, My Food Project

A few practical notes

The recipe does include one egg in the wrap batter, which lacto-ovo vegetarians will be fine with but strict vegetarians may want to know about before starting. Boiling the spinach first is what gives the wrap its smooth texture and vivid green colour — raw leaves would leave the batter gritty. And the sautéed-vegetable step is deliberately left open: Malhotra suggests "a spice mix of your choice," so use whatever seasoning your family already reaches for, from a simple salt-and-pepper toss to a full tandoori masala.
